warmup.q: Three machines each hold part of a log of payment events. To count each word, MapReduce, Google's system for running a job on many machines, runs 3 counting tasks that produce the final totals. (It calls them reducers.) The word approved appears on all 3 machines. How many of the counting tasks end up counting approved?
options: All 3, and a final step adds their answers together
Exactly 1, picked by hashing the word
Whichever counting task is free first
None: each machine counts its own words, and the totals are added up at the end
warmup.why: Every machine sends each word to the counting task that hash(word) mod 3 picks. That's a fixed formula that turns the word into a number from 0 to 2. The word gives the same number on every machine, so every machine sends its approved counts to the same task, which can total them alone. That's why no last step has to add up answers from different tasks. The second section builds this up.

sections.h: One file on many machines: big blocks, three copies each
sections.html:
Google's problem in 2003 was that its data didn't fit on one machine. A typical machine in its cluster had two 160 GB disks, its copies of the web filled many terabytes, and one disk needs hours to read even one terabyte. Let's spread the last lesson's files and sort over many machines, starting with the storage, built from the simplest version up.

Version 1: put each file on one machine. A 400 MB file of payments goes on machine 7. This breaks in two ways. A file bigger than one machine's disks can't be stored at all. And when machine 7 dies, the file is gone.

Version 2: cut every file into fixed-size pieces called blocks, and spread the blocks over many machines. Now a file can be bigger than any disk, and many machines can read one file at the same time. But a program that wants the file now needs to know where its blocks are. So one server, a machine whose job is to answer other machines' requests, keeps that list: each file's blocks, and the machines that hold each block. Data about data like this is called metadata. In the library, it's the catalogue that says which branch holds which book.

Version 3: keep copies. Machines still die, and their blocks die with them, so store every block on three machines. When one dies, the other two still serve the block, and the system makes a new third copy elsewhere. Keeping several copies is called replication.

That's the design of the Google File System (GFS, published in 2003), and of HDFS, the Hadoop Distributed File System. Hadoop is a free rebuild of Google's GFS and MapReduce that anyone can use. In HDFS, the machines that store blocks are DataNodes, and each block is a plain file on a DataNode's own disk. The metadata server is the NameNode, and every DataNode sends it regular block reports, lists of the blocks it holds. A block is 128 MB by default (dfs.blocksize; to be exact 128 MiB, 128 times 1,048,576 bytes), and each is stored three times (dfs.replication). A client, the program that wants the file, asks the NameNode where its blocks are, then reads the bytes straight from the DataNodes. File data never flows through the NameNode.

Why such big blocks? GFS used 64 MB. A 400 MB file is only 4 blocks of 128 MB, so the NameNode keeps 4 entries for it. The GFS paper reports that its metadata server needed only about 100 bytes per file. Each read also becomes one long stream in order, which is what disks do well. The flip side is that the server's memory caps the number of files, which is why millions of tiny files hurt HDFS (lesson 4 comes back to that).

The copies are placed on purpose. Machines sit in racks, cabinets that share power and a network switch, the box that links them. So HDFS puts the first copy on the machine that's writing, and the other two on two machines in one other rack. A dead disk, machine or whole rack loses no data.

Block locations had one more use. In 2004 the network was the scarce part: links of 100 Mb/s or 1 Gb/s carried far less than all the disks could read at once. So the scheduler ran each piece of work on a machine that already held a copy of its block. The data stayed put and the code travelled to it, like branches counting their own shelves. This is data locality. The library picture breaks here: a branch holds whole books, while HDFS cuts one file into pieces and keeps three identical copies of each piece.

Spark, a free program that runs one job across many cores or machines, still reads files this way. It cuts each input file into input partitions of at most 128 MB, set by spark.sql.files.maxPartitionBytes, and runs one task, one piece of work, per partition. Next, we'll compute something over those blocks.

try.title: Watch Spark cut a file into tasks
steps: From the labs folder, run SplitsDemo with the command below. The first run writes a 300 MB log file to bigdata/build/l02/ (a few seconds).
Predict first: into how many input partitions does Spark cut 300 MB with 128 MB pieces? And with 32 MB pieces?
Compare with the output. One partition is one task, the way one HDFS block got one piece of work in Google's design.

code.title: SplitsDemo.kt
code.html: package sfz.batch.l03.demo import java.io.File import kotlin.random.Random /** * Writes a 300 MB text file once, then asks Spark how many input partitions (tasks) it cuts the * file into: first with the default 128 MB split size, then with 32 MB. */ fun main() { val file = File("build/l02/auth-log.txt") if (!file.exists()) writeLog(file, targetBytes = 300_000_000L) val spark = demoSpark(threads = 2) println("file: %s, %,.0f MB".format(file.name, file.length() / 1e6)) for (split in listOf("128m", "32m")) { spark.conf().set("spark.sql.files.maxPartitionBytes", split) // the most bytes one task reads val partitions = spark.read().text(file.absolutePath).javaRDD().getNumPartitions() println("maxPartitionBytes=%-4s -> %d partitions, so %d map tasks".format(split, partitions, partitions)) } spark.stop() } /** Lines of made-up authorization log events, about [targetBytes] in total. */ private fun writeLog(file: File, targetBytes: Long) { file.parentFile.mkdirs() val words = listOf("approved", "declined", "refunded", "captured", "reversed", "card", "merchant", "issuer", "timeout", "retry") val rnd = Random(1) file.bufferedWriter().use { out -> var written = 0L while (written < targetBytes) { val line = (1..10).joinToString(" ") { words[rnd.nextInt(words.size)] } out.write(line); out.newLine() written += line.length + 1 } } }

try.expect:
file: auth-log.txt, 300 MB
maxPartitionBytes=128m -> 3 partitions, so 3 map tasks
maxPartitionBytes=32m  -> 9 partitions, so 9 map tasks

128m means 128 MiB, 134,217,728 bytes. 300 MB is 2.2 of those, so Spark makes 3 pieces; with 32 MiB it makes 9. The demo runs Spark with 2 cores on purpose. With many cores and a small file, Spark makes the pieces smaller so that every core gets work, though never below spark.sql.files.openCostInBytes (4 MB). So on a bigger machine you may see more partitions than the 128 MB rule suggests.

sections.h: Map, shuffle, reduce: counting across machines, one key at a time
sections.html:
Take the question the trace demo below answers: how many times does each status (approved, declined, refunded) appear in a log of payment events spread over three machines?

Version 1: every machine sends every status it reads to one machine, which counts. That's correct, and it falls over at scale, like driving every book to the central library. Change the question to "how many payments per card" over a billion cards. The counting machine now receives the whole input through one network link: 1 TB through a 1 Gb/s link (125 MB/s) takes over two hours. And it must keep a billion counters in memory, on a machine with 2 to 4 GB.

Version 2: use R counting machines, and give each one a share of the keys. A key is whatever you group by: a status, a card number, a shop. Every machine must send a given key to the same counting machine, without asking anyone. A hash function does exactly that: it turns a value into a number, and the same value always gives the same number. Java's String.hashCode() is one, and it gives the same number on every machine. Take that number modulo R, the remainder after dividing by R, and you get a machine number from 0 to R minus 1. In the library, every branch sends its notes for an author to the branch that owns that author, and works out the owner by itself.

Hadoop's rule is (key.hashCode() & Integer.MAX_VALUE) % R. A hash code can be negative, and a negative remainder isn't a machine number. So the & clears the bit that marks a number as negative.

Version 3: a counting machine now receives values for many keys, from many machines, in no useful order. If it sorts them by key first, equal keys sit next to each other, just like the first sort in the last lesson's pipeline. Then it can finish one key, write its result and move on, holding one key's values at a time.

That's MapReduce, published by Jeff Dean and Sanjay Ghemawat of Google in 2004. You write two functions. Map takes one input record and emits key and value pairs: the line approved declined approved becomes (approved, 1), (declined, 1), (approved, 1). Reduce takes one key with all its values and emits a result: approved with [1, 1, 1, 1, 1] becomes approved = 5. Map plays the part of the pipeline's awk, and reduce the part of uniq -c. A master program splits the input, runs one map task per block on a machine that holds it, and runs R reduce tasks, called reducers. Everything between map and reduce is the shuffle:

  1. Each map task splits its output into R parts with the partitioning rule, and writes the parts to its own machine's disk.
  2. Each reducer fetches its part from every map task over the network.
  3. Each reducer sorts what it fetched by key, calls reduce once per key, and writes one output file to the distributed file system: part-00000, part-00001, and so on.

A key always hashes to the same reducer, so one reducer sees every approved in the whole input, and reducers never need to talk to each other.

Failures are handled by running tasks again. The master checks on every machine. When one dies, its map tasks run again on another machine that holds a copy of the block. Even finished map tasks run again, because their output sat on the dead machine's own disk. Finished reduce tasks don't, because their output is already in the file system, in three copies. This works only because map and reduce are deterministic: run them twice on the same input and you get the same pairs. In a 1 TB sort, the paper's authors killed 200 of the 1,746 programs doing the work, a few minutes in. The job finished in 933 seconds instead of 891, 5% slower. Next, we'll make the shuffle carry less.

try.title: Trace a job phase by phase
steps: Run MapReduceTraceDemo with the command below. It runs the stepper's job and prints each phase.
Find approved in the three map lines. Check that every copy is tagged with the same reducer, r1.
Count the records in the shuffled line by hand from the map lines.

code.title: MapReduceTraceDemo.kt
code.html: package sfz.batch.l03.demo import kotlin.random.Random /** * A word count on three "nodes", printed phase by phase: map, partition, shuffle, reduce. * Run it with -Pargs=combine to add a combiner to each map task. */ fun main(args: Array<String>) { val combine = "combine" in args val splits = listOf( "approved declined approved", // block 1, stored on node A "approved refunded approved", // block 2, on node B "declined approved refunded", // block 3, on node C ) val reducers = 3 fun partition(key: String) = (key.hashCode() and Int.MAX_VALUE) % reducers // Hadoop's HashPartitioner // map: each node turns its own block into (word, 1) pairs, optionally combined val mapOutputs = splits.map { line -> val pairs = line.split(" ").map { it to 1 } if (combine) pairs.groupingBy { it.first }.fold(0) { s, p -> s + p.second }.toList() else pairs } mapOutputs.forEachIndexed { i, out -> println("map ${"ABC"[i]}: " + out.joinToString(" ") { (k, v) -> "($k,$v)->r${partition(k)}" }) } // shuffle: reducer r pulls partition r from every map node, then sorts by key val buckets = (0 until reducers).map { r -> mapOutputs.flatten().filter { partition(it.first) == r }.sortedBy { it.first } } buckets.forEachIndexed { r, b -> println("reduce $r gets: " + b.joinToString(" ") { (k, v) -> "($k,$v)" }) } val records = buckets.sumOf { it.size } val bytes = buckets.flatten().sumOf { it.first.length + 4 } println("shuffled: $records records, $bytes bytes") // reduce: one sum per key val output = buckets.flatMap { b -> b.groupBy({ it.first }, { it.second }).map { (k, vs) -> "$k=${vs.sum()}" } } println("output: " + output.joinToString(", ")) if (combine) atScale() } /** The same shuffle arithmetic on 20 map tasks of 50,000 events each, with and without a combiner. */ private fun atScale() { val rnd = Random(1) val statuses = listOf("approved", "declined", "refunded", "captured", "reversed") // key = status: five distinct keys per map task val byStatus = List(20) { List(50_000) { statuses[rnd.nextInt(statuses.size)] } } // key = payment id: every key is new val byPayment = List(20) { task -> List(50_000) { i -> "pay-%07d".format(task * 50_000 + i) } } for ((name, tasks) in listOf("count by status " to byStatus, "count by payment id" to byPayment)) { val plain = tasks.flatten() // one record per event val combined = tasks.flatMap { it.distinct() } // one record per key per map task println("%s without combiner: %,9d records %,10d bytes with: %,9d records %,10d bytes".format( name, plain.size, plain.sumOf { it.length + 4 }, combined.size, combined.sumOf { it.length + 4 })) } }

try.expect:
map A:    (approved,1)->r1 (declined,1)->r0 (approved,1)->r1
map B:    (approved,1)->r1 (refunded,1)->r2 (approved,1)->r1
map C:    (declined,1)->r0 (approved,1)->r1 (refunded,1)->r2
reduce 0 gets: (declined,1) (declined,1)
reduce 1 gets: (approved,1) (approved,1) (approved,1) (approved,1) (approved,1)
reduce 2 gets: (refunded,1) (refunded,1)
shuffled: 9 records, 108 bytes
output:   declined=2, approved=5, refunded=2

Every approved is tagged r1, on all three nodes, because String.hashCode() gives the same number everywhere. All nine pairs cross the shuffle. Each record costs its key (8 bytes here) plus 4 bytes for the count.

aside.title: What if one key has far more values than the others?
aside.html: Then one reducer gets most of the work, and the job waits for it: the slowest-machine problem from Why big data systems exist, all over again. Hashing spreads different keys over the reducers, but it can't split one key, because all the values for a key must meet in one place. In a log of payment events, approved might be most of the pairs. The combiner in the next section helps a lot here, because it shrinks a repeated key before it travels. When it can't help, the problem is called skew, and lesson 8 of this track deals with it.

video.title: One owner per key: how MapReduce counts across machines

sections.h: A combiner sends totals, and when that gives a wrong answer
sections.html:
Go back to version 1 and make it smarter. Let each machine count its own block first, and send totals instead of single pairs. A map task that read a million events would send five numbers for five statuses, not a million pairs. In the library, it's a branch that sends one note saying "Austen: 12" instead of twelve notes saying "Austen: 1". That trick is a combiner: it runs the reduce logic on one map task's output before anything crosses the network. In the last lesson's terms, it's a small hash map of counts on each map task.

It pays because every pair a map task emits costs disk space, network time and sorting time. The MapReduce paper points out that word counts follow a Zipf distribution: a few words are very common and most are rare. So each map task emits thousands of copies of the same few pairs, like (approved, 1). With a combiner, map task A turns (approved, 1), (approved, 1) into (approved, 2). The reducer still adds everything up; it just receives fewer, bigger numbers. In Hadoop, the combiner is often the reducer itself.

This is only correct when the answer stays the same however you group and order the pieces. Sum passes: (1 + 1) + 3, 1 + (1 + 3) and 3 + 1 + 1 are all 5. So do count, the smallest value and the largest. Mathematicians call such an operation associative (grouping doesn't matter) and commutative (order doesn't matter). Average fails. Say map task 1 sees two payments for a shop, 1,000 and 3,000 cents, and averages them to 2,000. Task 2 sees one payment of 10,000. The average of the two averages is 6,000, but the true average of the three payments is 4,667. Hadoop may also run a combiner zero, one or several times, so its answer can't depend on how often it runs.

A combiner must give the same answer however often it runs. For an average, carry the sum and the count, and divide once at the end. A combiner also needs repeated keys to pay off. If the key is a payment's number, each key appears once per map task, and the combiner saves nothing. Next, we'll see why MapReduce lost to Spark anyway.

try.title: Turn on the combiner
steps: Run the trace again with -Pargs=combine (command below). Compare the map lines and the shuffled line with the last run.
Read the two count by lines at the end. They do the same arithmetic on 20 map tasks of 50,000 events each.
Predict before you look: which key gains more from a combiner, the status or the payment's number?

map A:    (approved,2)->r1 (declined,1)->r0
map B:    (approved,2)->r1 (refunded,1)->r2
map C:    (declined,1)->r0 (approved,1)->r1 (refunded,1)->r2
reduce 0 gets: (declined,1) (declined,1)
reduce 1 gets: (approved,2) (approved,2) (approved,1)
reduce 2 gets: (refunded,1) (refunded,1)
shuffled: 7 records, 84 bytes

count by status      without combiner: 1,000,000 records 12,000,000 bytes   with:       100 records      1,200 bytes
count by payment id  without combiner: 1,000,000 records 15,000,000 bytes   with: 1,000,000 records 15,000,000 bytes

Same output, fewer records. On the tiny input the combiner saves 2 records out of 9. With 5 statuses and 50,000 events per task, it sends 100 records instead of a million. With payment numbers as keys it saves nothing, because no key repeats inside a task.

sections.h: Why MapReduce lost, and what survived
sections.html:
MapReduce wrote everything to disk on purpose. Map output went to each machine's own disk, and every job's final output went to HDFS, three copies. That made failures cheap to recover from, and it made long pipelines slow. Real work is rarely one job. A daily report built from five chained jobs wrote its in-between data to HDFS, three copies, and read it back, five times over. Machine learning was worse. There, a program improves a model by passing over the same data again and again. An algorithm that made 20 passes ran as 20 jobs, each reading the whole input from HDFS again.

Spark's answer came from the RDD paper (Resilient Distributed Datasets, 2012): keep the in-between data in memory between steps. When a machine dies, Spark works out the lost pieces again from their lineage, the recorded chain of steps that made them. It doesn't keep three copies of every result along the way.

Hadoop clusters faded after that, and in the cloud, rented storage took HDFS's place (the next section). Today Hadoop lives on mostly as libraries inside Spark, such as the S3A connector, the code that lets Spark read S3, Amazon's storage service. Nobody should start a new project by writing MapReduce jobs.

One more idea from the paper fixed the slowest machine. A job ends when its last task ends, and a machine with a bad disk can hold everything up. So near the end of a job, the master starts a backup task, a second copy of every task still running, and takes whichever copy finishes first. Two copies can't both win. A reduce task writes to a private temporary file and renames it to its final name when it's done. The file system's rename is atomic: it happens completely or not at all. With backup tasks turned off, the 1 TB sort took 1,283 seconds instead of 891, 44% longer, because five reduce tasks lagged for an extra 300 seconds.

Nearly all of these ideas survived:

MapReduce idea Where it lives now
Big blocks, one task per block Spark's input partitions, 128 MB by default
Move the code to the data Read fewer bytes: skip folders and files that can't match (lessons 4 and 5)
hash(key) mod R Spark's Exchange hashpartitioning(...), and the way Kafka picks a partition for a key
The combiner A partial count before the shuffle (partial_count)
Map output on the machine's own disk Spark's shuffle files, still written to local disk
Run a deterministic task again Spark working out lost pieces from lineage
One output file per reducer The part-00000 files in every Spark output folder
Backup tasks for slow machines Speculative execution (spark.speculation, off by default)
Write a temporary file, then rename Table formats that publish a change by swapping one pointer (lesson 11)

Kafka is a program that keeps logs of messages, split into partitions; the Messaging and logs track covers it. The local-disk row matters most. "Spark runs in memory, so it never touches disk" is wrong: Spark's own guide says a shuffle "generates a large number of intermediate files on disk". Lesson 7 of this track is all about the shuffle. Next, we'll see what replaced HDFS itself.

try.title: Find MapReduce inside a Spark plan
steps: Run SparkWordCountDemo. It counts the same three lines with Spark's DataFrame API. A DataFrame is a table of data that you change with calls such as groupBy. Before the result, the demo prints the physical plan: the tree of steps Spark decided to run.
Read the plan from the bottom up, like data flowing upward. Find the map side, the combiner, the shuffle and the reduce.
What is R, the number of reducers, in this plan? The demo's session sets spark.sql.shuffle.partitions to 4.

code.title: SparkWordCountDemo.kt
code.html: package sfz.batch.l03.demo import org.apache.spark.sql.Encoders import org.apache.spark.sql.functions.col import org.apache.spark.sql.functions.explode import org.apache.spark.sql.functions.split /** The same three-line word count in Spark, with the physical plan Spark chose for it. */ fun main() { val spark = demoSpark() val lines = spark.createDataset( listOf("approved declined approved", "approved refunded approved", "declined approved refunded"), Encoders.STRING(), ) val counts = lines .select(explode(split(col("value"), " ")).alias("word")) // map: one row per word .groupBy("word") // shuffle by word .count() // reduce (and combine) counts.explain() counts.orderBy("word").show() spark.stop() }

== Physical Plan ==
AdaptiveSparkPlan isFinalPlan=false
+- HashAggregate(keys=[word#6], functions=[count(1)])
   +- Exchange hashpartitioning(word#6, 4), ENSURE_REQUIREMENTS, [plan_id=15]
      +- HashAggregate(keys=[word#6], functions=[partial_count(1)])

The #6 and plan_id numbers vary between runs.

sections.h: Cloud storage replaced HDFS without being a file system
sections.html:
From about 2015, companies that rent their computers in the cloud, from Amazon, Microsoft or Google, stopped running HDFS. The 2021 Lakehouse paper dates the shift. Cloud object stores (Amazon S3, Microsoft's ADLS and Google Cloud Storage) began replacing HDFS because they keep data safe, keep copies in several data centres, and cost very little. An object store keeps objects, blobs of bytes that never change once written, under keys such as s3://lake/payments/dt=2026-11-07/part-00000.parquet. It hands them out over HTTP, the rules web browsers use to fetch pages.

HDFS put the data on the machines that compute on it, so storage and computing grow together, and someone has to run the NameNode. An object store separates them. You pay for storage by the byte and for computers by the hour, and data locality is gone. Growing past one machine, in the Foundations track, called this separating storage from compute. Losing locality stopped mattering much once networks inside data centres got fast: one rented Amazon machine can read S3 at up to 100 Gb/s.

What S3 gave up is the file system. A 2020 paper from the makers of Delta Lake, a table format, listed the gaps that hurt batch jobs. There are no folders, only keys that begin the same way, called a prefix. A LIST request, which asks for the keys with a prefix, returns at most 1,000 of them and takes tens to hundreds of milliseconds, so listing a million objects one request after another takes about 100 seconds. There's no rename: a rename copies and deletes every object, one at a time, so MapReduce's commit by atomic rename doesn't exist. There's no append, because an object is written whole. A request waits 100 to 200 ms for its first byte. And until December 2020, a LIST right after a write might not show it.

S3 has closed some of these gaps since. In December 2020 it became strongly consistent: once a write finishes, every read and every LIST sees it. In 2024 it added conditional writes, which succeed only if the object is still as the writer last saw it, or doesn't exist yet, so two writers can't both win. And in June 2025, S3 Express One Zone, a faster, separately priced kind of S3 that keeps its data in one zone (one group of data centres), gained an atomic rename. S3 Standard, the ordinary kind, still has neither atomic rename nor folders.

So modern engines stopped relying on either. A table format keeps its own list of a table's files, so nobody lists, and it publishes a change by swapping one pointer, so nobody renames. Lessons 11 and 12 build that on top of an object store.

refs.title: Delta Lake: High-Performance ACID Table Storage over Cloud Object Stores (Armbrust et al., VLDB 2020)
Amazon S3 now delivers strong read-after-write consistency (AWS, December 2020)
Amazon S3 adds conditional writes with If-Match (AWS, November 2024)
S3 Express One Zone supports atomic renaming of objects (AWS, June 2025)

opening:
Picture a city library on the night of its yearly count. The council wants to know, by morning, how many books it owns by each author. The books sit in forty branches across town.

The obvious plan is to bring every book to the central library and count it there, the way you'd count your shelves at home. With forty branches, that means a building too small for the books and a count still going next week.

The better plan sends the counting to the books. Each branch counts its own shelves and sends on short notes, never books. Google faced the same choice in 2003, with copies of the web on thousands of machines.

The last lesson, Batch on one machine, counted a log with five small programs, and a sort did the hard part. In this lesson, we'll spread the file and the sort over many machines, lose one on purpose, and see which of Google's ideas still run inside Spark, the engine this track uses most. Before we start, make a guess, and keep it in mind.
closing:
We started with a library that had to count forty branches by morning. The answer, counting where the books are and sending short notes, is MapReduce: map where the data sits, a shuffle that sends each key to one owner, then reduce. A lost note is written again from the books.

In jshell, the Java shell that comes with the JDK, type ("approved".hashCode() & Integer.MAX_VALUE) % 3. You get 1, the reducer the stepper gave approved. Change the 3 to a 4 and you get 3: change the number of reducers, and keys move.

Next, we'll give a folder of files a name and a list of columns, and find out how people asked questions in SQL instead of writing map and reduce.

compare.title: Word count in Hadoop MapReduce and in Spark

a.label: Hadoop MapReduce (Java)
a.title: TokenMapper.java and SumReducer.java
a.html: public class TokenMapper extends Mapper<LongWritable, Text, Text, IntWritable> { private static final IntWritable ONE = new IntWritable(1); private final Text word = new Text(); @Override protected void map(LongWritable offset, Text line, Context ctx) throws IOException, InterruptedException { for (String w : line.toString().toLowerCase().split("[^a-z]+")) { if (w.isEmpty()) continue; word.set(w); ctx.write(word, ONE); // (word, 1) } } } public class SumReducer extends Reducer<Text, IntWritable, Text, IntWritable> { @Override protected void reduce(Text word, Iterable<IntWritable> counts, Context ctx) throws IOException, InterruptedException { int sum = 0; for (IntWritable c : counts) sum += c.get(); ctx.write(word, new IntWritable(sum)); } } // in the driver: job.setCombinerClass(SumReducer.class); the reducer doubles as the combiner

b.label: Spark DataFrame (Kotlin)
b.title: the same job
b.html: val counts = lines .select(explode(split(lower(col("value")), "[^a-z]+")).alias("word")) .where(col("word").notEqual("")) .groupBy("word") .count() // partial count per partition, shuffle by word, final count counts.write().parquet("out/word_counts")

compare.note: The Hadoop version spells out the map and reduce functions, and you choose the combiner yourself. The Spark version says what you want, a count per word. Spark's planner then picks the same steps: a partial count on each partition, a shuffle by the word's hash, and a final count. The bigger difference is between jobs. Two chained Hadoop jobs talk through files in HDFS. Two Spark steps in one plan pass data along without writing it to the distributed file system. Only the shuffle, and spills when memory runs short, touch the local disk.

worked.title: Average payment per shop, with a combiner that stays correct

steps.say: The accountants want the average payment per shop across 3 billion payments. The shuffle is huge, so you want a combiner. The tempting one averages each map task's amounts. Check it on three numbers before you trust it.
steps.code: // 1. the tempting combiner: average per map task, then average the averages fun badCombine(amounts: List<Long>): Double = amounts.average() // map task 1 saw merchant m-17 twice: 1,000 and 3,000 cents -> 2,000.0 // map task 2 saw it once: 10,000 cents -> 10,000.0 // reducer: (2,000 + 10,000) / 2 = 6,000, but the true average is 14,000 / 3 = 4,666.67

steps.say: The fix is to carry what an average is made of. A partial result is a sum and a count, and adding two partials gives another partial. Addition doesn't care about grouping or order (it's associative and commutative), so the framework may combine in any order, any number of times.
steps.code: // 2. a partial aggregate that can be combined in any order data class SumCount(val sum: Long, val count: Long) { operator fun plus(other: SumCount) = SumCount(sum + other.sum, count + other.count) } fun map(merchantId: String, amountCents: Long) = merchantId to SumCount(amountCents, 1) fun combine(parts: List<SumCount>): SumCount = parts.reduce(SumCount::plus) fun reduce(parts: List<SumCount>): Double = parts.reduce(SumCount::plus).let { it.sum.toDouble() / it.count }

steps.say: Check it on the same numbers. Task 1 combines to (4,000, 2), task 2 to (10,000, 1). The reducer adds them and divides once.
steps.code: // 3. same input, right answer val result = reduce(listOf(SumCount(4_000, 2), SumCount(10_000, 1))) // 14,000 / 3 = 4,666.67

steps.say: Spark plans avg this way on its own. In its physical plan, the step before the shuffle is partial_avg, which keeps a sum and a count per partition, and the step after it does the division.
steps.code: // 4. in Spark: HashAggregate(partial_avg) -> Exchange hashpartitioning(merchant_id) -> HashAggregate(avg) payments.groupBy("merchant_id").agg(avg("amount_cents"))

lab.title: MapReduce word count by hand, then in Spark
steps: From the labs folder, run the tests with the command above. Tests are small programs that check your code and say what's wrong. All eleven fail for now. MapReduceJob.run at the bottom of MapReduce.kt is already written: it calls the pieces you're about to write, in order. Read it first.
Write WordCount.map, combine and reduce. Follow the rule in the KDoc, the comment above each function, exactly: lowercase first, then split on anything outside a to z.
Write HashPartitioner.partition with Hadoop's formula. One test feeds it polygenelubricants, a string whose hashCode() is Int.MIN_VALUE, the most negative Int.
Write Shuffle.shuffle: route every pair to its bucket, count records and bytes (the key's length in UTF-8, the usual way to store text as bytes, plus 4), then sort each bucket by key.
Run the tests. The job and combiner tests run your pieces together on 20,000 generated lines and compare the result with a plain groupingBy.
Write SparkWordCount.count with the DataFrame API and run all eleven tests. The last one reads Spark's physical plan and looks for your combiner and your shuffle in it.
hints: line.lowercase().split(Regex("[^a-z]+")) leaves an empty string when the line starts with a separator. Filter it out.
Kotlin's bitwise AND is the infix function and: (key.hashCode() and Int.MAX_VALUE) % reducers. Math.abs(Int.MIN_VALUE) is still negative.
pairs.groupingBy { it.key }.fold(0) { acc, kv -> acc + kv.value } sums per key in one pass.

For Spark: explode(split(lower(col("value")), "[^a-z]+")), then .where(col("word").notEqual("")) and .groupBy("word").count(). Kotlin lets you call a Java method named plus as +, but multiply and equalTo stay method calls.
lab.done: All eleven tests in MapReduceTest and SparkWordCountTest pass.

drill.title: Write the partitioner and the shuffle loop
drill.prompt: From memory, write partition(key, reducers) and the loop at the heart of shuffle: route each pair from each map task to its bucket, and count the bytes moved. Then say in one sentence why Hadoop clears the sign bit, the bit that marks a number as negative, instead of calling Math.abs.

answer.html: fun partition(key: String, reducers: Int): Int = (key.hashCode() and Int.MAX_VALUE) % reducers // never negative, same key -> same reducer fun shuffle(mapOutputs: List<List<KV>>, reducers: Int): Pair<List<List<KV>>, Long> { val buckets = List(reducers) { mutableListOf<KV>() } var bytes = 0L for (task in mapOutputs) for (kv in task) { buckets[partition(kv.key, reducers)] += kv bytes += kv.key.toByteArray(Charsets.UTF_8).size + 4 } return buckets.map { b -> b.sortedBy { it.key } } to bytes } // Math.abs(Int.MIN_VALUE) overflows back to Int.MIN_VALUE, so a key like // "polygenelubricants" would get a negative bucket; clearing the sign bit can't go negative.

recap: HDFS cut files into 128 MB blocks and stored each one on three DataNodes, with one NameNode keeping the map of where every block lives.
MapReduce runs map, then a shuffle, then reduce. The shuffle sends each pair to reducer hash(key) mod R, keeps map output on the map machine's own disk, and lets each reducer fetch and sort its keys.
A combiner adds up on the map side. It's only safe when grouping and order don't change the answer (sum, count, min, max); for an average, carry (sum, count).
Failures are handled by running deterministic tasks again, including finished map tasks whose output died with their machine.

The limit: MapReduce sent every job's output through disk and HDFS, so chains of jobs were slow. Spark kept the ideas (input partitions, Exchange, partial counts, shuffle files on disk) and dropped the rest.

Object stores such as S3 replaced HDFS in the cloud. They have no folders and, in S3 Standard, no atomic rename, so table formats keep their own file lists and publish a change by swapping one pointer.

explain.prompt: A friend says: "Spark replaced MapReduce because Spark runs in memory and never writes to disk." Explain what's right and what's wrong in that sentence, using the shuffle.
explain.answer: The right part: MapReduce wrote every job's output to HDFS, three copies. A chain of jobs, or an algorithm that passes over the data many times, paid that cost again and again. Spark keeps in-between data in memory between the steps of one plan, and rebuilds lost pieces from lineage instead of keeping copies. The wrong part is "never writes to disk". A shuffle still works the way MapReduce's did. The map side splits its output by the hash of the key and writes shuffle files to its local disk, and the reduce side fetches them over the network. Spark's own guide says a shuffle makes many in-between files on disk. So the shuffle is still the expensive step, and fewer or smaller shuffles are still how you make a Spark job faster.

deeper.html:
Backup tasks in Spark. Spark kept MapReduce's backup tasks under the name speculative execution. It's off by default (spark.speculation=false). Turn it on and Spark 4.3 checks every 100 ms. Once 90% of a stage's tasks (a stage is a group of tasks that run the same step) have finished (spark.speculation.quantile), it starts a copy of any task that has run more than 3 times as long as the median (spark.speculation.multiplier). Whichever copy finishes first wins, and the other is stopped.

It suits clusters with busy neighbours and flaky disks. It's useless when a task is slow because of its data. If one key holds a third of all rows, a copy of that task reads the same third and is just as slow. That problem is skew, and lesson 8 of this track handles it. Speculation also leans on the atomic rename of section 4. A task whose output is a file publishes it once, but a copy of a task that writes rows into a database or sends an email does it twice. That's why it's off by default.

More of S3's recent changes. S3 Express One Zone, launched in November 2023, answers in single-digit milliseconds, up to 10 times faster than S3 Standard. It gained appends in November 2024 and the atomic RenameObject in June 2025. In a test by Classmethod, renaming a 10 GB object that way took about 0.7 seconds, against about a minute for copy and delete. Conditional writes came in two steps: If-None-Match (write only if the key is new) in August 2024, then If-Match (write only if the object hasn't changed, a compare-and-swap) in November 2024. And in December 2024, S3 Tables added managed tables in Apache Iceberg, the table format lesson 11 uses, where S3 itself does the compaction and clean-up that lesson 12 describes.

Why Snowflake built on S3. Snowflake, a company that sells a database for analysis in the cloud, built it on S3 instead of running its own HDFS. Its 2016 paper says S3's availability and durability were hard to beat, despite slower requests.

GFS's honesty about trade-offs. The GFS paper is worth reading for how plainly it trades consistency for speed. Its metadata server kept less than 64 bytes per 64 MB piece: one cluster of 227 machines, holding 155 TB, needed only 60 MB of server memory in all. Its record append writes a record at least once, so readers have to cope with duplicates and padding. Batch jobs that read GFS files were written to skip both, the same at-least-once thinking that a program reading from Kafka needs.
